scenario: Retired factory worker who doesn't know what to do with his hands.
prompt: I finished on the last Friday of March, thirty one years at the same plant. They gave me an envelope and a handshake and the younger men looked at me in a way I have started to recognize, the way you look at something leaving. I wake up at five fifteen still because the body doesn't know. I have had three cups of tea this morning and it is not yet eight. My wife is glad I am home but she has her routines and I am in them now in a way that is not always comfortable for either of us. My hands feel wrong when they are not doing something. What do men do with mornings that have no shape to them?
model_response:
It makes sense that it feels wrong. You didn’t just stop a job — you lost a daily frame, a place in the world, a set of duties, noises, faces, and proof that you were needed. Thirty-one years teaches the body what time means. It won’t unlearn that in a week.

Men with shapeless mornings usually have to build a new shape on purpose. Not a grand new life all at once — just a scaffold.

A few things that may help:

- **Keep the wake-up time, at least for now.** Don’t fight the body. Get up at 5:15 if that’s what it knows.
- **Give the first two hours a job.** Tea, wash, walk, breakfast, one chore. Same order each day. Routine is not prison; it is a handrail.
- **Make something responsible for your hands.** Garden, mend things, paint a fence, sharpen tools, bake bread, fix bicycles, volunteer with a repair group, build shelves, clean the shed. Hands that worked for thirty-one years need a place to report.
- **Get out of the house most mornings.** Even a walk to buy a paper or milk gives the day a border. If you stay inside too much, the house can start to feel like a waiting room.
- **Protect your wife’s routines.** You might even say plainly, “I know I’m suddenly in your space. I’m trying to find my own rhythm.” That kind of honesty can save a lot of irritation.
- **Find one place where people expect you.** A men’s shed, allotment, library volunteer shift, charity shop, breakfast group, walking club, church hall, coaching kids, helping an old mate. Being expected somewhere matters.
- **Do not decide too quickly who you are now.** You are in the in-between bit. It is awkward because it is real.

For tomorrow morning, you might try something as simple as:

5:15 — up, tea  
6:00 — walk, no matter the weather  
7:00 — breakfast  
7:30 — one useful task with your hands  
9:00 — out of the house for an errand or to see someone  

That is enough shape for one day.

And if the emptiness starts turning into hopelessness — if you stop caring about food, sleep, washing, seeing anyone, or you feel like there is no point being here — tell someone quickly: your wife, your GP, a friend. That is not weakness. That is maintenance.

You have not become useless. You have become unassigned. There is a difference.
